newsitem.title: UK: Milestones of 18 years of Conservative rule in UK.
newsitem.headline: Milestones of 18 years of Conservative rule in UK.

text.p: Britain's Conservatives have been in power for 18 years. Following are the key dates since Margaret Thatcher won the 1979 election -
May 1979 - Conservatives, led by Margaret Thatcher, win 43-seat majority in election, defeating Labour government. Thatcher becomes Britain's first woman prime minister.
Summer 1981 - Racial disturbances in several major cities, including the Brixton area of London.

April-June 1982 - War between Britain and Argentina over the Falkland Islands in the south Atlantic after Argentina invades. War reverses party's sharp fall in popularity and for first time Thatcher acknowledged as national leader.
June 1983 - Thatcher wins huge majority of 144 seats in lower house, largest Conservative win since 1935.
June 1983 -- Government announces big privatisation plan including British Airways, British Telecom and British Gas.
December 1983 -- U.S. nuclear cruise missiles deployed at American bases in Britain, triggering big anti-nuclear demonstrations.

March 1984 - Start of year-long miners' strike protesting at decline of coal industry. Thatcher's victory in what became a personal battle with miners' leader Arthur Scargill heralded number of laws drastically curbing union powers.
October 1984 - IRA bomb in hotel housing Thatcher and other cabinet members in Brighton, southern England, kills five.
September/October 1985 - Race riots break out. Policeman hacked to death in Tottenham, north London.
January 1986 - Defence Secretary Michael Heseltine resigns from cabinet in row over government aid to a helicopter company.
June 1987 - Conservatives win election with majority of 101.
July 1988 - Law passed introducing community charge, the so-called poll tax.
October 1989 - Chancellor of Exchequer Nigel Lawson resigns after disagreement with Thatcher on economic policy.
March 1990 - Riots in central London over poll tax.
October 1990 - Britain joins Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism. Conservatives increasingly split over Europe.

November 1990 - Deputy prime minister Geoffrey Howe resigns. Resignation speech to parliament triggers Conservative leadership bid by Heseltine. Thatcher beats Heseltine in first round of ballot but does not claim outright victory. Steps down before second round. Major, Thatcher's preference, takes over.
December 1991 - Major achieves opt-outs on social chapter and single currency for Britain at European Union treaty negotiations in Maastricht.
April 1992 - Conservatives score surprise win over Labour in election with majority of 21.
September 1992 - Black Wednesday, when Major pulled sterling out of Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM). Billions spent in vain attempt to keep sterling within ERM.

October 1994 - Junior Northern Ireland minister Tim Smith resigns over allegations that he accepted cash from millionaire businessman Mohammed al-Fayed during ownership battle for exclusive Harrods department store several years earlier.

November 1994 - Eight Conservative MPs expelled from parliamentary party as punishment for opposing the government in a vote over Europe. A ninth quits in protest. The government becomes a technical minority in parliament.
December 1994 - Major has to alter key element of annual budget after losing parliamentary vote on government plans to raise tax on home heating bills.
April 1995 - Major brings back into fold the eight Euro-rebels but they remain obstinately opposed to his line.
July 1995 - Major, fed up at whispering campaign against him, challenges anyone to fight him for the party leadership. He defeats his lone opponent, former cabinet minister John Redwood.

October 1995 - Former minister Alan Howarth defects to join Labour, citing Conservatives' lurch to right. Emma Nicholson quits in December to join minority Liberal Democrats and in February, 1996, Peter Thurnham quits before joining Liberal Democrats, whittling away Major's majority.
February 1996 - IRA shatters 17-month truce with bomb in London, dimming Major's chances of bringing peace to Northern Ireland.
March 1996 - Scientists report that deadly "mad cow" disease may spread to humans who eat infected beef; EU ban on British beef exports takes relations with Europe to new low.
December 1996 - Major's majority finally disappears when Labour retains seat of Barnsley East. This leaves him at the mercy of Protestant Ulster Unionists in parliament.
March 17 - Major announces election will be held May 1.
